Turf built for Reunion's guest turnover

Turf for a Reunion vacation rental prices at the standard $8–$18 per square foot, typically $10–$16, as of September 2026, since the material and base don't change for a managed home. What changes is the spec: a lawn that has to photograph well and hold up between one guest group checking out and the next one checking in, usually with nobody local watching it in between.

Reviewed by Luis Austin, owner · Last reviewed September 21, 2026

Say you manage a rental with a 900 sq ft backyard

Say you manage a Reunion rental with a 900 sq ft backyard that currently turns brown between waterings when the booking calendar is light and nobody's requesting extra irrigation. At $8–$18 a foot, converting it runs roughly $7,200 to $16,200, with most jobs this size landing near $10–$16 a foot, or about $9,000 to $14,400, plus a modest premium for the heavier-duty product on the main walking path from the gate to the pool deck. Once the heads are capped, that yard no longer depends on someone remembering to run a hose or request a mid-stay watering visit, and the association submittal for a rental home follows the same review process as an owner-occupied one, just routed through whoever holds power of attorney or management authority for the account.

Zoning that already expects rental use

Osceola County zones short-term rental activity through a Short Term Rental Planned Development designation, and a large share of Reunion sits inside that framework, which is part of why so much of the resort's housing stock runs as managed rentals rather than year-round residences osceola.org. That zoning status doesn't change anything about the turf standard itself; it just means the property manager, not necessarily the owner, is often the one coordinating the install and the review submittal.

Why green is the only color decision the state rule addresses

Florida's turf standard specifically allows green synthetic turf, which settles the one product question that would otherwise vary from job to job on a Reunion rental: color stays consistent across every listing photo taken over the years, regardless of season or which crew handled a repair. That consistency matters more for a property marketed through rotating photos on a booking site than it does for a family home nobody photographs professionally. Beyond color, the product decisions that actually vary, pile density, infill type, backing spec, get made the same way they would for any residential lot.

Choosing a product that survives a booking calendar

A rental home's yard sees a rotating set of guests who didn't pick the landscaping and won't be the ones dealing with a worn patch six months later, so we lean toward a heavier face weight and a denser stitch on the paths guests actually walk, from the driveway to the pool gate, rather than spreading the same light-duty product evenly across the whole lot. A photo-ready lawn that stays flat and green between cleanings matters more for a listing's reviews than it does for most owner-occupied yards.

Grading a side yard to match a pool deck someone already built

Many Reunion rental homes already have a paved pool deck in place before a side-yard turf job ever gets scheduled, and the new base has to grade into whatever slope that existing deck established rather than starting from a blank lot. Getting the transition wrong leaves a low spot right where the two surfaces meet, which is exactly where a rolling cooler or a suitcase crosses from the yard to the patio. Matching the base's one to two percent grade to an existing structure takes more field measuring than laying out a border on open ground with no prior construction to work around.

Warning guests who have never stood on hot turf before

A family visiting Reunion on vacation has no local habit of checking turf temperature before letting kids run across it barefoot, unlike a homeowner who learns quickly. Full summer sun pushes the surface to 120 to 150°F, and a rinse drops that 30 to 50 degrees within minutes, but that only helps if someone tells the guest to do it. A line in the house manual about hosing the yard before pool time, left where an out-of-town family will actually read it, does more good on a rental than the same fact would on a house where the residents already know it.

Extra nails where the luggage crosses, not everywhere

Rather than tightening perimeter spacing across an entire Reunion rental yard, the corner where the entry path meets the driveway, the specific spot suitcases and coolers roll across on their way in, gets the closest nail spacing on the job. The rest of the perimeter, along a side fence nobody drags anything across, holds to a standard residential spacing. Concentrating the extra anchoring on one identifiable stretch does more for a rental's actual wear pattern than spreading a uniform tightened spacing across corners that will barely see foot traffic at all.

Getting infill topped off before the season, not during it

A property manager's standing vendor for a Reunion rental portfolio does better scheduling an infill check ahead of the busiest booking stretch of the year than waiting for a fixed quarterly date that might land in the middle of it. Topping off zeolite or silica sand before demand peaks means the yard is at full depth exactly when the most guests will be on it, rather than catching up on infill after a season's worth of heavy traffic and hose rinsing has already thinned it out. The timing matters as much as the frequency here.

One less thing for a manager to schedule

Once a Reunion rental's lawn goes synthetic, the in-ground irrigation heads under it get capped under the state's turf standard, which means the watering schedule Toho assigns by address no longer applies to that section of the yard at all the state's capping requirement. For a property manager juggling turnover across several Reunion addresses, one less irrigation zone to track between guest stays is a real, if small, operational win, on top of the yard simply not going brown during a slow booking week.

Questions people ask

Can a property manager submit the ARC application instead of the owner?

Usually, if the manager has documented authority on file with the association. Check with the resort's property owners association about what paperwork it needs before assuming a manager can submit on the owner's behalf.

Does turf reduce water bills on a Reunion rental with bundled utilities?

For sections where water and sewer are folded into the association fee rather than billed by usage, the savings show up as reduced irrigation demand on the shared system rather than a lower individual bill, which still matters for a community managing water costs overall. The vacation rental turf page covers product choices for a high-turnover yard.
